findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled as soon as the request completes
findings.body: All four write paths (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) spawn a goroutine whose context is derived from the incoming request context via `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. net/http cancels the request context as soon as the handler returns, which will normally happen before (or shortly after) the goroutine gets scheduled. The derived context is therefore already cancelled, so the legacy SQL store call will abort with `context canceled` and the 10s timeout is effectively meaningless. The whole point of mode 3 is to keep legacy storage in sync as a safety net, so this silently drops most legacy writes. The goroutine needs a context detached from the request lifetime (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a fresh background context carrying the requester/identity values) before applying the timeout.

findings.title: Errors from the asynchronous legacy writes are never logged
findings.body: In the goroutines for Create (line 55), Delete (line 112), Update (line 139) and DeleteCollection (line 165) the error returned by the legacy store is only fed into a duration histogram's `isError` label; nothing is logged. The previous implementation logged these failures (`unable to create object in legacy storage`, `could not delete from legacy store`, ...). With mode 3 this means legacy and unified storage can silently drift apart with no operator-visible signal other than an aggregate metric label, making divergence impossible to diagnose per object. Log the error together with the object name/kind.

findings.title: Spawned goroutines have no panic recovery, so a legacy store panic kills the process
findings.body: The four `go func()` blocks (lines 50, 108, 134, 161) call into legacy storage without a `defer recover()`. Panics inside an HTTP handler are recovered by the apiserver's panic middleware, but a panic in a detached goroutine terminates the entire Grafana process. Since these goroutines run arbitrary legacy storage code (including validation callbacks passed in from the request), a single bad object can now crash the server instead of failing one request. Add a recover (and log) wrapper around the goroutine bodies.

findings.title: Delete records the object name in the `kind` metric label, causing unbounded cardinality
findings.body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Each distinct deleted object therefore creates a new histogram label value in the storage duration metric, so the time series count grows without bound with the number of deletes, bloating the Prometheus registry and scrape payload. It also makes the metric unusable for comparing with the other operations. Should be `options.Kind`.

findings.title: Create error path records a legacy duration for a storage failure
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. The failure came from unified storage, not from legacy, so the error is attributed to the wrong backend and the storage histogram never records the failed call. This makes the dual-writer dashboards report phantom legacy errors and hide unified-storage errors. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

findings.title: Update error path records a legacy duration for a storage failure
findings.body: `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` is called when `d.Storage.Update` returns an error. As in Create, a unified-storage failure is recorded against the legacy backend's histogram and the storage histogram misses the failure entirely, producing misleading metrics. Should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

findings.title: DeleteCollection goroutine records the legacy call under the storage metric
findings.body: Inside the async goroutine, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is reported with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)`. This double-counts the storage histogram (it was already recorded at line 159 for the real storage call) with the legacy latency, and the legacy histogram records nothing for delete-collection, so legacy failures for this operation are invisible. Should be `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`.

findings.title: Delete injects the bare logger into the context instead of the enriched one
findings.body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses `d.Log` rather than the `log` created on line 96. Every downstream component that pulls the logger out of the context via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` loses the `name`, `kind` and `method` values, which is inconsistent with every other method in this file and makes delete-related log lines unattributable.

findings.title: Legacy Update is now driven by the raw objInfo instead of the object written to storage
findings.body: The previous implementation wrapped objInfo (`&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}`) so legacy received exactly the object that was persisted to unified storage. Now the unmodified `objInfo` is handed to `d.Legacy.Update`, so legacy re-evaluates the update against the *legacy* copy of the object. For PATCH/apply requests the transformers are re-run against a different base object, and for requests carrying a resourceVersion the precondition is checked against the legacy resourceVersion (which is not the same value space as unified storage), so the legacy write can fail with a spurious conflict. Combined with the fact that the error is only counted in a metric, this silently diverges the two stores.

findings.title: NotFound from unified storage now aborts the legacy delete, leaving orphaned legacy rows
findings.body: The old Delete explicitly tolerated `apierrors.IsNotFound` from unified storage and still issued the legacy delete. The new code returns early on any error, so an object that exists only in legacy (e.g. written before the mode switch, or whose unified write failed) can never be deleted: reads come from unified storage, so the row is invisible, and the delete never reaches legacy. Consider keeping the NotFound passthrough so legacy cleanup still happens.

findings.title: Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write, and leak unsynchronized goroutines
findings.body: The new tests use a single `mock.Mock` instance shared by `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock`, so a call to legacy is indistinguishable from a call to storage, and no test asserts that the legacy store was written at all. The central behaviour of mode 3 (write to unified, then asynchronously mirror to legacy) is therefore untested; the mislabeled metrics and the context-cancellation problem in dualwriter_mode3.go would not be caught. In addition, nothing waits for the spawned goroutine, so the mock is invoked after the subtest finishes - any future assertion on legacy calls will be flaky, and an unmatched expectation would panic in a background goroutine and abort the whole test binary. Use separate mocks for legacy and storage and add synchronization (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup signalled from the legacy mock) so the async write can be asserted deterministically.

findings.title: Duplicate go.work.sum entry added
findings.body: `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod h1:...` is added at line 409 although the identical line already exists a few lines above (line 405). The duplication indicates the file was hand-edited or generated with a mismatched toolchain rather than produced by `go mod tidy`/`go work sync`; the whole set of added hashes is unrelated to this dual-writer change and should be dropped or regenerated.
